description:
Equipo LifePlants
LifePlants busca explorar cómo la tecnología, los datos y las plantas pueden aportar a soluciones de sostenibilidad, tanto en la Tierra como en futuros entornos espaciales. Buscamos personas interesadas en construir y aprender en equipo.
summary: NEXUS: Last Horizon is a free 3D browser game in which players become an astronaut running a small base at the Moon’s south pole, near the region NASA’s Artemis program plans to explore. Players design and operate the base. They build a habitat, a greenhouse and solar power, deploy robots that mine regolith on their own, and drive a rover into a dark crater to collect ice. Every choice is a real trade-off. During lunar darkness the battery cannot power everything, so players decide what to switch off. Solar storms modeled on real flares recorded by NASA DONKI force the crew into the shelter. A guided first mission turns mistakes into understanding: a commander on Earth compares plans before you act, and a final report explains what you learned. The game addresses the challenge by making the engineering of living on the Moon playable and visible: power, water, oxygen, food and radiation. It matters because it brings NASA data and Artemis-era science to students and families in Spanish and English, on any phone or computer, with nothing to install.
details:
What it does. NEXUS: Last Horizon is a free 3D game that runs in any web browser, on phones and computers, with nothing to install. The player is an astronaut at a small base on the Moon’s south pole, near the region NASA’s Artemis program plans to explore. Commander Rivera talks to them by radio from Earth. The game trains young people the way astronauts train: through simulation, decisions under pressure and a debrief.

How it works. Players build and run the base:

  • a habitat with a regolith berm against radiation,
  • a greenhouse where a plant needs the right water, light and temperature,
  • solar masts and batteries,
  • robots that mine regolith on their own,
  • a rover that drives into a dark crater to collect ice.

Every choice is a trade-off. When the terrain blocks the Sun, the battery cannot power everything, so the player decides what to switch off. Solar storms are built from real flares from the last 60 days in NASA DONKI: the flare class sets how strong the storm is and how much warning the crew gets. Live NOAA GOES proton data shows the radiation Earth is measuring right now. Real meteor showers (IMO calendar) bring more micrometeoroid impacts. Every number is credited on an in-game “NASA Data” screen with its source and time; if there is no internet, a dated copy is used and the game says so.

Learning by design. Mission 1 is a guided, 2-minute scenario: a lunar darkness and a solar storm. At any moment the player can pause and ask “What should I do?”. The commander then runs each possible plan through the same game engine and shows what would happen before the player commits. At the end, a report explains what happened, what the player learned (for example, why the Moon offers no protection from solar radiation) and one tip for next time. Failing is part of learning.

Benefits and impact. It brings real space-weather data and Artemis-era science to students, teachers and families, in Spanish and English, on the devices they already own, including low-end phones. It turns abstract ideas (energy versus power, radiation shielding, life support, food production) into decisions players can feel.

Tools.

  • Languages and frameworks: TypeScript, Three.js (WebGL), Vite, Vitest (346 automated tests) and GSAP for the landing page.
  • Hosting: Netlify and Cloudflare. The code is open on GitHub.
  • Art: all 3D models are built in code; there are no downloaded assets.
  • AI assistance: we used Claude (Anthropic) as a coding and writing assistant.

Creativity. The Sun in the game is the real Sun, and the commander is a “what-if” simulator rather than a hint button. Game saves are stylized PNG mission cards with the data hidden inside the image, so players can share and reload them without an account.

Factors we considered.

  • Performance on cheap phones (capped resolution, adaptive quality).
  • Touch controls and full screen.
  • Honest data labels: live versus saved copies, and measured near Earth, not on the Moon.
  • Kid-friendly language and accessibility (reduced motion, large touch targets).
  • Bilingual text that switches live.
  • No NASA logos or insignia.
